title: What films are the best examples of the Kishōtenketsu story structure?

commenti.body:
The most obvious example is Kurosawa’s classic Rashomon. If you want to see a film that is explicitly written using this structure- I highly suggest starting there.

I'd actually be interested in comparing the Kishōtenketsu structure with Western murder mysteries. I think that you could make parallels with the *ten* - the "twist" - and the revelation of the true murderer. In a good murder mystery, you then must recontextualise the events you've seen up to that point in the light of this new information. And in a lot of mysteries, once the truth is out, the drama is largely over, and it's more about how the people deal with the new status quo - *ketsu*.

Tangential nitpick — *kishōtenketsu* was **not** the "classic structure of Chinese, Korean, and Japanese narratives." It was a retrospective analysis of the structure of Tang-dynasty poems, but we don't have any records of it earlier than the Yuan dynasty (i.e. several centuries after the poems were written). There were a few references to it as a possible narrative structure in 19th-century Japan, but it didn't really become a big part of how East Asians thought about story structure until the 20th century. 

Of course, most East Asian films were made in the 20th century or later, and several screenwriters have explicitly stated that they thought about their narratives in terms of *kishōtenketsu*, so it can definitely be something to consider when analysing the narrative structure of an East Asian film. But it isn't "classical" — *kishōtenketsu* narrative structures are basically a modern invention.

What an interesting post! This is the first time that I heard about this concept, and I am going to start paying attention to reading more about it.

I don't have any examples to give you, but I'm going to tune in for later additions and clarifications.
Also, the movie to make Toshiro Mifune a known face.

Funnily enough, I had never heard that term in my life before last week ([Baader-Meinhof phenomenon](https://www.dictionary.com/e/tech-science/baader-meinhof-phenomenon/) style) when I was skimming through the screenwriter Shinobu Hashimoto's book *Compound Cinematics -  Akira Kurosawa and I*.

I have zero knowledge on the topic myself and I didn't quite understand what Hashimoto was trying to say, but I can quote the passage for those interested. Hashimoto had just written a second attempt at what would eventually become the *Seven Samurai* script called *The Lives of Japanese Swordsmen* and Kurosawa had some comments on it:

> When Mr. Kurosawa finally finished reading the manuscript of 297 half-sheets, he let out a breath. A long sigh. Long enough to make me wonder just how much air the human body could possibly hold. Then, through the lingering note of his sigh he murmured, “Hashimoto … Scenarios require *kishotenketsu*, it would seem.” 

> *Kishotenketsu*, a venerable piece of scenario terminology, referred to the introduction (ki), development (sho), climax (ten), and conclusion (ketsu). The term itself, however, was musty, so we said Start, Development, Climax, and Last, using the English words for all but Development (for which we preferred the modern “tenkai”). Since these were divided and placed into four boxes, we called *kishotenketsu* “the four boxes” or even “big box” for short—as in “What happened to the big box?” or “How’s the big box?” In any case, it meant that the structure (assemblage) of a scenario had four indispensable elements and stages. With a self-deprecating, bitterish smile Mr. Kurosawa said, “Trying to string together climaxes from beginning to end to make a movie was woefully wrongheaded in the first place, I guess.” 

> I sank into silence. Halfway through, I’d felt a strange something I’d never experienced before; it was the overstrain and contradiction of completely ignoring the four stages of assembling a story, the “four boxes,” and composing a film out of nothing but climaxes. So dumb a folly—my mind went dead silent like a vacuum. Not just *A Samurai’s Day*, but now *The Lives of Japanese Swordsmen*, was kaput. 

> Eventually, I managed to utter, “Right … no way a film can be all climax from beginning to end.”

I remember many years ago watching Sans Soleil by Chris Marker and thinking that many of the small sections, even individual shots, could fit the kishōtenketsu structure. But I was young and dumb back then so I don't know if that holds up today.

My Neighbour Totoro is the prime example for me, yes. 

​

And now I'm going to throw a weird one, and let me know if it makes sense or not. I'm afraid that, with enough mental gymnastics, every story can be forced to fit any narrative structure (that's why I'm not super passionate about McKee and Syd Field an all that, it's a good tool but that's it, because if I twist it enough I can convince you Andy Warhol's Empire fits the Hero's Journey or whatever).

But anyway, yesterday I saw Beau Travail by Claire Denis, and it kind of fits? There is the introduction, a really long middle section where "nothing happens" in terms of western story structure, but a tension is clearly building up. Then there is a twist, or a conflict with 2 characters, a conflict that we are used to see in other films maybe at the first third or at the middle point, never later than that, but in Beau Travail it happens at the last 20minutes or so. Then those last minutes are just the consequences of that conflict.
Now my unrelated question is: why is the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon called that? What has it to do with Baader and Meinhof?

https://www.dictionary.com/e/tech-science/baader-meinhof-phenomenon/

> The Baader-Meinhof phenomenon is named for the Baader-Meinhof Gang, a 1970s German terrorist group. The name of the phenomenon is thought to have been coined by Terry Mullen, who explained his experience with it in a 1994 letter to a Minnesota newspaper. Mullen said he started using the name due to the experience of having discussed the Baader-Meinhof Gang and then encountering a mention of the group in the newspaper the next day, despite the fact that the group hadn’t been newsworthy for many years. Mullen applied the term to the experience of encountering a word or idea in print within 24 hours after first learning it. Today, the term is typically used more broadly.

There is an anime movie - ["Your Name."](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt5311514/) \- it brushes quite close to Kishōtenketsu in my opinion, though it does have some foreshadowing that kind of softens the Ten part but I think the mood shift is quite strong.

I read that ["Parasite"](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt6751668/?ref_=nv_sr_srsg_0_tt_8_nm_0_q_Parasite) has Kishōtenketsu structure, though I didn't see it.
